catalog_quote: Klemtoon. Een klemtoon als in de aanverwante talen, namelijk op de voorlaatste syllabe van een meerlettergrepig woord, bestaat in het Boesangsch niet; wel een licht accent op de laatste syllabe van zulk een woord, bv.: hapi' — dij këloenan — mensch. In uitdrukkingen en zinnen valt dat accent op de laatste lettergreep van het laatste woord, bv.; Toean alang kĕm tĕngaran aoer Kĕlĕpoea: de heer die het bestuur voert over de Boven Kapoeas; ... Is het laatste woord van den zin éénlettergrepig, dan valt uit den aard der zaak hierop de klemtoon, bv.: Baha tè' lòh, nja' aoe pah: rijst er nog steeds, (maar) het zout is op. Een en ander sluit niet uit het, waar noodig en gewenscht, accentueeren van een bepaald woord van den zin, omdat in dat woord een hoofdgedachte besloten ligt, bv.: Héran ika sang moedik: wanneer gaat ge op reis (stroomopwaarts).

new_statements.translation: Stress. A stress accent as in the related languages, namely on the penultimate syllable of a polysyllabic word, does not exist in Busang; there is, however, a light accent on the last syllable of such a word, e.g. hapi' 'thigh', këloenan 'person'. In expressions and sentences that accent falls on the last syllable of the last word [...]. If the last word of the sentence is monosyllabic, the stress naturally falls on it [...]. None of this excludes, where necessary and desired, accentuating a particular word of the sentence because a main idea is contained in that word.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No penultimate word stress of the Malay/Kayan type; polysyllabic words carry only a weak accent on the final syllable, and in connected speech the prominence falls on the final syllable of the last word of the phrase/sentence; emphatic (focus) accent on any word is possible.
new_statements.exceptions: None lexical; author notes only that sentence-final monosyllables take the accent and that contrastive emphasis can override placement.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent described as 'licht' (weak) and final; in phrases/sentences it is realised on the last syllable of the last word, i.e. largely phrase-final prominence. Based on the Busang spoken by the Uma' Aging (Mendalam, Upper Kapuas) plus Upper Mahakam material; impressionistic 1910 description by a colonial administrator.
new_statements.identity_note: Barth 1910 (Glottolog files it under Kayan-Busang [bfg]) states (Inleiding pp. XIII-XIV) that the Busang of his dictionary is the variety used as tribal language ('stamtaal') by the Uma' Aging of the Mendalam River, Upper Kapuas (West Borneo), where he began learning it, supplemented with words learned on the Upper Mahakam; he treats it as one language ('Boesangsch') spoken by the Mendalam 'Kayans', the Upper Mahakam Busang tribes (Uma' Suling, Uma' Lekuwe, Uma' Urut, Uma' Tuwan, etc.), most Middle Mahakam tribes and the Uma' Leken of the Apo Kayan, noting Middle-Mahakam dialect differences (d>r, s>h, final -e>-ei). The Mendalam component may overlap with what Glottolog calls Mendalam Kayan [xkd, mend1267]; the stress statement is given for 'het Boesangsch' as a whole.
